metadata.title: Week 1 Project Progress: Understanding the Humanitarians AI Website Repo
metadata.purpose: Fellow-style weekly project progress video for Week 1
metadata.format_note: Canonical GitHub submission beat sheet. Portrait is a derivative render, not a separate submission source folder in this package.

beats.narration_text: Hi I am Rushali and the video is about how the Humanitarians AI website repository is structured. In Week 1, my main progress was understanding the codebase well enough to make future changes safely.

props.command: I wonder what Humanitarians AI fellow Rushali has been working on lately…
output: Week 1 focus: understand the codebase first.
Key layers: app, components, app/api, lib, public, assets.

beats.narration_text: Most of my first week was not about shipping a big feature. It was about reading the repo, tracing how pages and components connect, understanding branch based workflow, and building a mental map so I would know where edits belong before changing anything.

props.title: The first job was understanding the system
props.subtitle: Before changing live code, I needed a reliable map of how the repo and workflow fit together.

beats.narration_text: At a high level, I now think about the repository in layers. The app folder defines routes and pages, components holds reusable interface pieces, app slash api and lib handle server side logic and shared data code, and folders like public and assets support what the site serves. That structure made the project much easier to navigate.

props.title: The repo works as connected layers
props.subtitle: Routes, reusable UI, server logic, and static assets each have a different job.
props.sparkLine: Know which layer you are changing.
props.footer:
page change -> app/
shared UI -> components/
server logic -> app/api + lib/
static files -> public + assets/

beats.narration_text: If I were onboarding a new contributor, I would start with app. In Next.js, many folders inside app map directly to URLs, and page dot tsx creates the page. Then I would look at layout dot tsx for shared wrappers, and components for the reusable pieces that those pages assemble.

props.title: Start with the route, then inspect the shared shell
props.subtitle: A URL points to a page file, and that page is wrapped by layout and assembled from shared components.
props.sparkLine: URL to file to shared UI.

beats.narration_text: The api side works differently from page routes. Files under app slash api are server handlers that return data or perform actions, often with shared logic coming from lib. I also kept track of support folders like public, assets, scripts, and sql, because they matter whenever the task involves static files, automation, or database related work.

props.title: app/api handles requests, while lib and support folders back it up
props.subtitle: These routes process data and actions instead of rendering a visible page.

beats.narration_text: The main takeaway from this week is that understanding the repo first is real progress. The strength was building a reliable mental model before editing live code. The next step is to use that map to make targeted changes, debug issues faster, and help future contributors ramp up more quickly.

props.title: Understanding first was the real progress
props.subtitle: A clean mental model turns future code changes into targeted work instead of guesswork.
props.footer: The value of Week 1 was not just reading files. It was building a map that makes debugging, onboarding, and future code changes faster and safer.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you are new to this repository, start by tracing one real page from its URL to app, then to layout, then to the components and any api calls behind it. That one exercise will quickly show you where most future changes belong.

props.command: Pick one real page in this repository and trace it from the URL to app, then to page.tsx, layout.tsx, the components it imports, and any app/api or lib logic that supports it. Summarize where you would make a change safely.
